name: Valley Forge
desc: Valley Forge was the winter encampment of the Continental Army under George Washington in eastern Pennsylvania, along the Schuylkill River, during the Philadelphia campaign of the American Revolutionary War. Unable to defend Philadelphia after his defeat at the Battle of Brandywine, Washington led his 12,000-man army into winter quarters there in December 1777, approximately 18 miles northwest of the city. The army faced a disastrous supply crisis, and an estimated 1,700 to 2,000 soldiers died from disease, possibly made worse by malnutrition and cold, wet weather. Baron Friedrich von Steuben, a Prussian drill master, instituted a training program before the army marched out in June 1778.

name: George Washington's crossing of the Delaware River
desc: George Washington's crossing of the Delaware River, on the night of 25–26 December 1776, was the first move in a surprise attack by the Continental Army on the Hessian forces garrisoned at Trenton during the American Revolutionary War. Washington, the army's commander-in-chief, led a column from Pennsylvania across the icy river to New Jersey at McConkey's Ferry, in weather that turned from rain to sleet and snow. Other planned crossings in support were called off or ineffective, leaving about 2,400 men for the attack. After defeating the Hessians under Johann Rall in the Battle of Trenton, the army crossed back to Pennsylvania with its prisoners and captured stores.

name: Battle of Trenton
desc: The Battle of Trenton was a short American Revolutionary War battle fought on the morning of 26 December 1776, in Trenton, New Jersey. After crossing the icy Delaware River the previous night, George Washington led 2,400 men of the Continental Army against a garrison of about 1,400 Hessian auxiliaries commanded by Colonel Johann Rall. The Hessians, who had no long-distance outposts or patrols, were caught off guard; they lost 22 killed, including Rall, and 896 captured, while the Americans suffered two deaths on the march and five wounded. Coming after defeats in New York and a retreat through New Jersey, the victory raised the army's waning morale and inspired re-enlistments.

name: Great Frost of 1709
desc: The Great Frost, as it was known in England, or Le Grand Hiver in France, was an extraordinarily cold winter in Europe in 1708–1709, the coldest European winter of the past 500 years. William Derham recorded a low of −12 °C at Upminster, near London, on the night of 5 January 1709. France was particularly hard hit: the famine that followed is estimated to have caused 600,000 deaths by the end of 1710. During the Great Northern War, winter storms and frosts killed thousands in the Swedish army invading Russia, contributing to the Russian victory at Poltava the following summer.

name: Siege of Leningrad
desc: The siege of Leningrad was a military blockade of the Soviet city of Leningrad, present-day Saint Petersburg, by Germany and Finland on the Eastern Front of World War II; it lasted 872 days, and the city was never captured. Land routes to the rest of the Soviet Union were cut on 8 September 1941, and the Germans decided to bomb the city and starve its inhabitants. Many residents starved during the winter of 1941–1942; the siege caused an estimated 1.5 million deaths, from a prewar population of 3.2 million, and some historians have classified it as a genocide. Supplies came across Lake Ladoga, in winter over the Road of Life on the ice, until the siege was fully broken on 27 January 1944.

name: River Thames frost fairs
desc: The River Thames frost fairs were held on the frozen tideway of the River Thames in London in some winters, from at least the late 7th century until the early 19th. Most took place between the early 17th and early 19th centuries, during the Little Ice Age, when the river was wider and slower and was further impeded by the 19 piers of the medieval Old London Bridge. The first known fair was in 695, and the term was first used of the fair of 1608. During the Great Frost of 1683–84 the Thames was completely frozen for two months. The last fair began on 1 February 1814 and lasted four days, with printing presses on the ice; the old bridge was removed in 1831.

name: Treaty of Ghent
desc: The Treaty of Ghent was the peace treaty that ended the War of 1812 between the United States and the United Kingdom, signed on 24 December 1814, in the city of Ghent, now in Belgium. It restored the pre-war borders of June 1812. The five American commissioners were led by John Quincy Adams; the British at first demanded an Indigenous buffer state in the area from present-day Ohio to Wisconsin, which the Americans refused to consider. News of the treaty took a month to reach the United States, and in the meantime American forces under Andrew Jackson won the Battle of New Orleans on 8 January 1815. The treaty took effect in February 1815, when ratified copies were exchanged in Washington.

name: Amundsen's South Pole expedition
desc: Amundsen's South Pole expedition, led by the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen, was the first to reach the Geographic South Pole, on 14 December 1911. Amundsen had planned an Arctic drift in Fridtjof Nansen's ship Fram, but changed his goal in secret and revealed the Antarctic destination to his crew only on leaving Madeira in September 1910. From his base, Framheim, in the Bay of Whales, he set out in October 1911 with four companions, using skis and sled dogs and reaching the polar plateau by the Axel Heiberg Glacier. They arrived five weeks ahead of the British party led by Robert Falcon Scott, whose five men died on their return journey, and returned safely to their base in January 1912.

name: Apollo 8
desc: Apollo 8 was the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and the first human spaceflight to reach the Moon, flown from 21 to 27 December 1968. Its three astronauts, Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and William Anders, travelled 68 hours to the Moon and orbited it ten times without landing; they were the first humans to see and photograph its far side and an Earthrise. On Christmas Eve they read the first ten verses of the Book of Genesis in a television broadcast. The mission, the first crewed launch of the Saturn V rocket, ended with a splashdown in the northern Pacific Ocean and paved the way for Apollo 11 in July 1969.

name: A Christmas Carol
aka: A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas
desc: A Christmas Carol is a novella by Charles Dickens, first published in London by Chapman & Hall in 1843 with illustrations by John Leech. It tells of Ebenezer Scrooge, an elderly miser who is visited by the ghost of his former business partner Jacob Marley and the spirits of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come, and becomes a kinder man. Dickens was inspired by a visit to the Field Lane Ragged School for London's street children. Published on 19 December, the first edition sold out by Christmas Eve, and thirteen editions had appeared by the end of 1844. The book has never been out of print, and Dickens gave public readings of it from 1849 until 1870, the year of his death.

name: The Nutcracker
desc: The Nutcracker is a two-act classical ballet by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, first performed on 18 December 1892 at the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre in Saint Petersburg, in a double premiere with his last opera, Iolanta. Its plot, set on Christmas Eve, adapts Alexandre Dumas's 1844 retelling of E. T. A. Hoffmann's 1816 story The Nutcracker and the Mouse King. The libretto was by Marius Petipa; whether he or his assistant Lev Ivanov choreographed the first production has been debated. The first performance was not deemed a success. Since the late 1960s the ballet has been danced by many companies, especially in North America; its score is noted for its use of the celesta.

name: Wright Flyer
desc: The Wright Flyer is the aircraft that made the first sustained flight by a manned, powered and controlled heavier-than-air machine, on 17 December 1903. Built and flown by Orville and Wilbur Wright, it is a single-place biplane with a 12 horsepower gasoline engine driving two pusher propellers. They flew it four times at what is now Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina: Orville's first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet, and the fourth, by Wilbur, covered 852 feet in 59 seconds before gusts wrecked the machine. After a long dispute between Orville and the Smithsonian Institution it joined the Institution's collection in 1948 and is displayed in Washington, D.C.
